name: ClauseLens known failure patterns (rental)
disclaimer: These patterns are advisory comparison knowledge about clauses that commonly lead to tenant disputes or unexpected cost. They are not universal legal rules and they are not a statement of what a court would do.

patterns.description: Damage is a trigger for a deduction, but the agreement does not define it.
patterns.why_it_matters: An undefined damage trigger can be read broadly enough to cover ordinary use, so the amount at stake is unclear until the word is defined.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a definition of damage that excludes normal wear and tear, and ask a lawyer to review enforceability in the relevant jurisdiction.

patterns.description: The agreement does not set a joint inspection before deposit deductions.
patterns.why_it_matters: Without an inspection step, the tenant has no agreed record of condition at move-out before money is withheld.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a joint inspection and a signed note before any deduction.

patterns.description: The agreement does not say when the remaining deposit must be returned.
patterns.why_it_matters: Without a return date, the tenant cannot point to an agreed deadline for the balance that remains after deductions.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a stated refund timeline after move-out and itemized deductions.

patterns.description: A deposit can be retained without an itemized list of deductions.
patterns.why_it_matters: A single unitemized retention makes it hard to tell which rupees relate to which item of loss.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for itemized deductions tied to an inspection note.

patterns.description: A deduction clause does not distinguish ordinary wear from damage.
patterns.why_it_matters: If the deduction clause never points to a wear-and-tear definition, ordinary use can be treated as a deductible event.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask the damage clause to exclude normal wear and tear by reference to the definition in the agreement.

patterns.description: The tenant is given open-ended responsibility for repairs, including structural work.
patterns.why_it_matters: Open-ended repair duties have no stated ceiling, so a defensible amount often cannot be calculated.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a split between structural repairs and day-to-day upkeep, and mark the clause for legal review if the ceiling is still unclear.

patterns.description: A small or unclear charge is tied to severe default language.
patterns.why_it_matters: Severe default language can raise consequences beyond the stated fee, even when the fee itself is small.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for the charge to stay a stated fee, with a grace period where relevant, and without treating that fee alone as a serious default.

patterns.description: Rent can change without a stated percentage, amount, or date.
patterns.why_it_matters: An open-ended increase has no defensible figure until the formula and the date are written down.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a fixed percentage or amount and the date it applies.

patterns.description: Ending the agreement early depends on a compensation formula that is broader than the comparison standard.
patterns.why_it_matters: Early-exit compensation can equal multiple months of rent even when the clause sounds like a routine condition.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a defined cap and for the notice clause to govern the exit. Consider legal review of the lock-in.

patterns.description: The agreement does not say who pays which utility.
patterns.why_it_matters: Unassigned utility charges can become a surprise invoice with no formula in the agreement.
patterns.suggested_review_action: Ask for a list of utilities and who pays each one.
